summary:
Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013), in force 1 May 2013, criminalises same-sex sexual conduct through sections 67, 68 and 71. Section 67 makes the act complete on penetration with no defence of consent, section 68 makes attempts liable to imprisonment for up to five years, and section 71 makes keeping a place of resort for homosexual acts liable to up to seven years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records the headline penalty as five years. The same sections also prohibit heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex, and a 2007 decision, Police v Poi, defined the act as penetration of the anus by the offender's penis, whether of a male or female victim.

The offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, so it reaches a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship. On that basis Samoa should be treated as a jurisdiction where that conduct is a criminal offence carrying a custodial penalty.

Enforcement is reported to be absent. In June 2010 the Samoa Law Reform Commission recommended repealing all criminal penalties for such acts in private between consenting adult males, recording majority public support for the change; the Government rejected that recommendation and a reported decriminalisation proposal in 2011.

No Samoan law targets gender expression itself. The Crimes Act 2013 removed the provisions of the predecessor Crimes Ordinance 1961 that criminalised males "impersonating" females in a public place, provisions that had been used against transgender women and gender-diverse people. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that the new act was in force that week and that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the repeal. The same reporting records that the community was not then agitating for repeal of the sodomy provisions, and decriminalisation on that front did not follow.

Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 addresses crimes motivated by gender identity, and the same provision covers crimes motivated by sexual orientation. This sits alongside, rather than in place of, the criminal prohibitions in the Crimes Act.

There is no recognition of same-sex relationships. Prime-ministerial statements in 2012, 2013 and 2017 rejected same-sex marriage on Christian and traditional grounds. Samoa rejected first-cycle Universal Periodic Review recommendations from Canada, France and Norway to repeal criminalisation, and rejected all second-cycle recommendations except one on reducing violence, stating that decriminalisation was not possible because of cultural sensitivities and Christian beliefs.

The social climate is described in the sourced material as markedly more accepting of gender diversity than of homosexuality: "Samoan society tends to be very tolerant of being transgender, but not of homosexuality." Fa'afafine, assigned male at birth and explicitly embodying both gender traits, has been recognised as a gender identity or role since at least the early 20th century, and the Ombudsman's first National State of Human Rights Report, released in August 2015, referred to fa'afafine as "the third gender that has always existed in Samoa" and noted their carrying of both men's and women's family roles.

On care, the Mental Health Act 2007, published 2 February 2007, states that people are not to be considered mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation, and prohibits conversion therapy by mental health professionals.
tangentialFactors:
APTN reported on 9 May 2024 that a convening in Nadi, Fiji brought together gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua and Papua New Guinea, documenting the regional spectrum of MVPFAFF+ identities of which Samoa's fa'afafine community is one part, alongside fakaleiti in Tonga and fakafifine in Niue. A visitor encountering these terms elsewhere in the region is meeting a shared identity family rather than a Samoan peculiarity.

Schmidt's 2001 article in Intersections, "Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa", glosses the term as "in the manner of a woman" and argues that fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality and transgenderism discourses, with the diaspora community abroad serving as a contact zone. The framing a visitor meets may therefore be shaped by that exchange rather than by Samoan usage alone.

The UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet of August 2015 lists the fa'afafine of Samoa, American Samoa and Tokelau among the diverse pre-colonial gender identities of the region that are "important parts of the cultural treasure of the region". Samoa also signed the UN joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.

In 2026 Samoa held its first LGBTQ Pride Week, with residents and allies gathering to celebrate the community. This is a public-event fact about social climate and does not alter the statutory position described above.
localsOnly:
Section 20(2) of the Labour and Employment Relations Act 2013 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment policies, procedures or practices. The provision addresses sexual orientation rather than gender identity, and its application to fa'afafine workers is not documented in the sourced material.

The Samoa Fa'afafine Association filed a stakeholder report for Samoa's Universal Periodic Review at the 39th session in 2021, titled "The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa", describing the culturally specific third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documenting lived experience in support of non-discriminatory policy and legislation.

During the UPR process Samoa stated that fa'afafine, gays and lesbians were integral members of society and heirs to family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, while maintaining that sexual orientation was a sensitive issue given the religious and cultural beliefs of mainstream society and requiring education and sensitisation for acceptance.

The Samoa Fa'afafine Association has set its own priorities in public statements: in 2017 it named "the promotion of human rights and the reduction of discrimination and violence based on gender identity" as its priority, and in 2018 stated that "marriage is the least of our worries when you don't have a job, it's not a priority". The association is also described as fostering collaboration between the fa'afafine and LGBTQ communities while balancing Samoan values with Western influences, and it regards the anti-gay laws as hindering full incorporation of both fa'afafine and gay and lesbian Samoans.
outOfScopeNotes:
A Reuters feature on Samoa's third gender, balancing sex and religion, returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be retrieved; its contents are unverified here.

The APTN socio-economic study covering Samoa is published as a scanned image document, so its findings could not be extracted and are not reflected in this assessment.

The inventory contains no sourced information on entry or visa rules, on gender markers in passports or other identity documents, or on whether document markers are flagged at the border. It also contains no sourced account of airport screening treatment specific to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers, such as pat-downs or secondary screening triggered by binders, packers or breast forms, and no sourced information on targeted anatomy inspection.

Nothing in the inventory addresses access to gender-affirming care for visitors, the lawfulness or availability of such care, or rules on facilities and restrooms. These remain not sourced rather than resolved either way.

Enforcement detail is thin. The sourced material states that the Crimes Act provisions are not enforced, but the inventory contains no case data, prosecution counts or police-practice documentation to test that claim, and no record of how section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 has been applied.

The inventory carries no trans-specific violence figures for Samoa, and none can be derived from it. No comparison against a general homicide rate is possible from these sources.
